scope: fixed32 remaining BESD-N02-B01 and BESD-N04-B01 seed replacements; accepted i017 and i019 remain unchanged

replacements.learningObjective: Choose a resource representation that exposes bounded freshness and distinguishes an absent asset from a temporarily unavailable metadata read.

question.prompt: A media catalog serves metadata for assets. Each asset has a stable asset ID; metadata may lag behind ingestion by up to 30 seconds, and a missing asset must be distinguishable from a failed catalog read. Which contract best fits that read?
constraints: The catalog is the authority for asset identity.
A metadata projection may lag by at most 30 seconds.
A missing asset and an unavailable origin are different outcomes.

options.text: Expose a read-only `/assets/{id}` resource with its projection age and distinct not-found and unavailable outcomes.
Treat a missing metadata projection as a refresh request: have the read start ingestion, return pending, and ask callers to poll until it appears.
Expose the catalog table row layout directly and require every caller to infer whether a missing row means no asset or a failed read.

feedback.reason: The stable asset ID gives callers a durable resource identity, while the projection timestamp makes the 30-second lag interpretable. A read remains a query: it does not start ingestion, and the response distinguishes absence from origin failure.
feedback.details:
Treat `/assets/{assetId}` as the contract boundary, not as a promise that every ingestion path is synchronous. The response can include the metadata projection version or timestamp so callers can apply the stated 30-second limit. A genuine missing asset is a not-found result; an origin failure is an availability error, not a successful empty representation. Starting ingestion from GET would make retries and prefetching trigger work, while exposing table columns would couple clients to persistence details. If callers needed read-your-writes immediately after ingestion, this bounded projection contract would need a stronger completion or version rule.

Boundary and reversal: If the product later requires immediate read-your-writes after ingestion, callers need an accepted-operation or source-version contract in addition to this bounded read.

messages.text: A read now initiates work and conflates a missing asset with an accepted refresh.
Storage schema leaks implementation details and the required outcome distinction is lost.

replacements.learningObjective: Define an event identity and application ordering field so receivers can suppress redelivery and reject older shipment state without treating delivery order as guaranteed.

question.prompt: A carrier integration emits shipment status changes. Delivery can repeat the same update, and a delayed earlier update may arrive after a newer one. Which event contract lets the logistics service preserve the shipment’s latest state?
constraints: A carrier event has a stable source and event ID across redelivery.
Each shipment has a monotonically increasing revision assigned by the carrier.
The receiver may see events out of order.

options.text: Give each event a stable source/ID and shipment revision; deduplicate repeated IDs and apply only newer revisions.
Rely on the transport to deliver each event once and in order, then overwrite the shipment state with every arrival.
Use receiver arrival time as the revision and overwrite state on each delivery, assuming later received means later occurred.

feedback.reason: Event identity handles the same occurrence being redelivered; the carrier revision handles distinct updates arriving out of order. The receiver can therefore suppress duplicates and refuse to move the shipment backward.
feedback.details:
The two identifiers answer different questions. CloudEvents source plus id can identify a repeated event, while the scenario’s carrier revision is an application-level ordering field for one shipment. The event format alone does not guarantee ordered delivery or exactly-once processing. Persist the highest applied revision with shipment state; a duplicate event becomes a no-op, and a lower revision cannot replace a later status. If a carrier cannot provide a monotonic revision, the integration needs a different source-defined ordering rule before claiming that it can reconstruct latest state.

Boundary and reversal: If the carrier guarantees a single ordered stream per shipment and assigns no revisions, the consumer can rely on that explicit contract; no such guarantee is present here.

messages.text: The stated repeated and delayed deliveries violate both assumptions.
Arrival order measures network timing, not the carrier’s state order.

replacements.learningObjective: Use a representation version as a write precondition so concurrent document edits produce a visible conflict rather than silent last-write-wins.

question.prompt: A document editor reads revision 41. Another editor may save revision 42 before the first editor submits its changes. The server must not silently overwrite the intervening edit. Which save contract meets that requirement?
constraints: Every document representation carries a strong version validator.
A write based on an older revision must leave the newer document unchanged.
The client can present a conflict and let its user merge.

options.text: Submit the read version as an If-Match precondition; write only if it remains current, otherwise return a conflict.
Replace the document unconditionally with the revision 41 copy, letting the last save win and avoiding a merge response.
Have the client compare a fresh GET locally, then send an unconditional PUT to avoid a conflict response.

feedback.reason: A server-side precondition closes the race between checking the revision and applying the edit. A mismatch becomes an explicit conflict instead of a lost update.
feedback.details:
An ETag or equivalent strong revision token can be sent as an If-Match precondition. RFC 9110 describes conditional requests as a way to prevent lost updates; the origin evaluates the condition as part of applying the state-changing method. The client can then merge or ask the editor to resolve the conflict. A client-side GET/compare followed by an unconditional write is not atomic, and unconditional replacement makes the stale revision indistinguishable from a current one. If concurrent edits should merge automatically, that is a different domain contract and must define the merge semantics.

Boundary and reversal: If the product later adopts a deterministic merge model, version preconditions may still detect concurrent inputs, but conflict presentation can be replaced by the specified merge behavior.

messages.text: A stale full representation would erase the concurrent edit.
The state can change between the client’s check and its write.

replacements.learningObjective: Place the stock invariant in one atomic reserve command at the inventory authority, not in a preceding availability query.

question.prompt: An inventory service has exactly one unit left. Two buyers can try to reserve it at the same time; the service must never confirm both reservations. Which API behavior preserves that result?
constraints: The available count can change between a browse and a reservation.
Both buyers can submit before either receives a response.
A losing buyer should learn that no reservation was created.

options.text: Make the stock check and decrement one atomic reserve command; return a reservation or a conflict with none created.
Read stock first, then submit an unconditional reservation using that count; refresh only if another buyer reports a race.
Accept a cached positive count and let a reconciliation job repair negative inventory after checkout completes.

feedback.reason: The availability query cannot serialize competing buyers. The reserve command must couple the stock check and state change at the authority, and a conflict must mean no reservation was accepted.
feedback.details:
The command contract names the authoritative outcome: reservation ID on success, or a conflict that does not create a reservation. The state change must enforce `available >= requested` and decrement in the same atomic operation or equivalent serialization boundary. A read followed by a write leaves a race window; a cache is suitable for display only when the scenario permits stale estimates, not for deciding whether the invariant holds. If partial reservations are allowed, the response must state the accepted quantity explicitly rather than imply the full request succeeded.

Boundary and reversal: If inventory is split across independent authorities, a single atomic reserve is unavailable; the product would need to define allocation, compensation and the user-visible partial outcome.

messages.text: Both buyers can read the same final unit before either write occurs.
A later repair does not undo an already accepted oversell.

replacements.learningObjective: Model one-time module completion as an idempotent desired-state resource rather than an incrementing submission counter.

question.prompt: A learner can retry a completion submission after losing the response. Completing one module should remain complete once, even if the same submission reaches the service again. Which contract expresses that state?
constraints: Completion is a binary state for each learner and module.
Repeating the same completion request must not add another unit of progress.
The service owns the durable progress record.

options.text: Address completion by learner and module; set it complete so repeating the same request leaves the stored state unchanged.
Post a progress increment for every accepted delivery and use a client timestamp to identify likely duplicate submissions.
Ask the client to suppress a retry after timeout and assume the server did not commit without an acknowledgment.

feedback.reason: A set-to-complete resource models the invariant directly: applying the same request twice leaves the same completion state. The API does not infer that a timeout means the first write failed.
feedback.details:
Use a stable resource identity such as learner plus module, and define the operation as setting completion, not adding a count. Repeated submissions then converge on the same durable state without requiring each network attempt to be a new event. An increment endpoint turns a retry into duplicate progress; client-side retry suppression cannot distinguish a lost response from an unapplied request. If the domain later allows multiple separately credited attempts, those attempts need their own identities and rules rather than changing the meaning of completion.

Boundary and reversal: If progress is based on independently graded attempts, represent each attempt as a separately identified record; this question’s one-time module-completion rule would no longer apply.

messages.text: A replay becomes additional progress because the operation is an increment.
The client cannot know whether the server committed before the response was lost.

replacements.learningObjective: Pin each checkout quote to an immutable price revision so a retry cannot silently substitute a newer price.

question.prompt: A catalog operator publishes price revisions while checkout requests are in flight. A quote may be retried for five minutes, and the customer must see the same quoted amount throughout that interval. Which contract should checkout use?
constraints: A published price revision is immutable.
A quote remains valid for five minutes and must keep the amount returned when it was created.
A newer revision may become current while an existing quote remains valid.

options.text: Create an immutable quote bound to one price revision; reads retain its amount until the quote expires.
Resolve the product’s latest price each time the quote URL is read, even if the customer already received an earlier amount.
Have the client send its displayed amount at purchase time and accept it without validating the referenced revision.

feedback.reason: The quote must retain the exact immutable revision that produced its amount. Looking up “current price” again would change a still-valid quote; accepting an unverified client amount would detach the purchase from catalog authority.
feedback.details:
Treat product price revisions as immutable facts and the quote as a distinct resource that pins one revision. Its five-minute expiry gives a clear boundary after which checkout may require a new quote. A mutable latest-price lookup is appropriate for discovering today’s price, but not for reinterpreting an existing quote. The client can display the amount, yet the server must resolve and retain the authoritative revision when creating the quote. If prices must become effective immediately even for existing quotes, the scenario’s five-minute validity promise must change.

Boundary and reversal: If the business requires emergency price withdrawal to invalidate open quotes, define an explicit revocation rule and return that outcome rather than silently replacing the pinned amount.

messages.text: The same quote changes meaning during its validity period.
The amount can be stale or altered and is not bound to the catalog revision.

replacements.learningObjective: Define when a credential revocation response is success, given that copied credentials may still be presented to the service.

question.prompt: An identity service revokes a credential. The API promises that once revocation returns success, requests using that credential are rejected; authorization decisions are made by the service, not by offline clients.
constraints: The API promises that a token is rejected for protected requests after revocation succeeds.
The server makes the authorization decision for each protected request.
A client may still hold a copied token after the revocation response.

options.text: Persist a new credential epoch before success; protected requests compare the token against the current epoch.
Return success when a revocation message is queued, then let authorization nodes update from the message later.
Tell the active client to delete its token, while server checks continue to accept any otherwise valid copy.

feedback.reason: The service must make the revoked state effective for protected requests before it reports success. A queued eventual update or client-only logout leaves copied credentials usable after the promised boundary.
feedback.details:
Model revocation as a state-changing command with an explicit completion point. The identity service records the revocation and only then returns success; every later protected request consults authorization state that reflects that completion. The implementation may use an epoch, status record, or another durable mechanism, but it cannot acknowledge success while copied tokens remain accepted. If immediate enforcement is unavailable, return a distinct pending outcome or change the promise. Deleting a token from one device does not invalidate copies held elsewhere.

Boundary and reversal: If the product permits a measured revocation delay, the response can state that weaker bound and the checks can enforce it; immediate post-success rejection is the premise here.

messages.text: A request can still be authorized after the API has promised revocation.
A copied or offline token remains usable because the server does not enforce revocation.

replacements.learningObjective: Propagate a caller deadline through synchronous route computation and stop work when the caller no longer needs the result.

question.prompt: A dispatch screen requests a route preview and waits at most 300 ms. A route calculation can exceed that bound, and the result is discarded if it arrives after the screen moves on. Which request contract controls wasted work?
constraints: The caller’s 300 ms wait bound is explicit.
A late route preview has no durable value.
The server can observe cancellation or deadline expiry.

options.text: Set a realistic request deadline, propagate its remaining budget to downstream calls, and cancel computation when the request expires.
Leave the request open until route computation eventually finishes and let the client abandon the response locally.
Persist every preview as a long-running job and require polling even though late results are discarded.

feedback.reason: A propagated deadline makes the 300 ms budget meaningful across the call chain. Because a late preview has no durable value, cancellation is preferable to persisting work and polling for it.
feedback.details:
The client deadline expresses how long it is willing to wait; downstream calls should receive the remaining budget rather than reset a fresh timeout at each hop. When the deadline expires, the server should cancel work it spawned where possible. This does not guarantee that every computation can stop instantly, so resource limits still matter. A durable operation resource is useful when work must continue after the caller disconnects; the scenario explicitly says previews are discarded, so that contract would preserve unwanted work.

Boundary and reversal: If dispatchers need to retrieve the route after leaving the screen, the result becomes durable work and should use an explicit operation resource with its own lifecycle.

messages.text: Server and downstream work continue after the only consumer has gone away.
Durable work adds state and retries for a result the scenario does not need to retain.

replacements.learningObjective: Return a rollout decision without requiring each mobile client to implement the changing cohort rule.

question.prompt: A feature rollout assigns accounts by a rule that operations may revise during the release. Old and new app versions call the same evaluation endpoint; each needs the result for the signed-in account, while the assignment rule itself is maintained by the service.
constraints: The decision is evaluated for one authenticated account and one feature key.
Operations can revise the assignment rule without releasing a new app.
Clients need a stable decision and the rule revision used for it.

options.text: Evaluate the account against the current server rule and return the decision with its rule revision.
Return the rollout percentages and bucketing algorithm; have every app version calculate the account decision locally.
Let each app choose and cache a random local result until the next release.

feedback.reason: Clients need an account-specific evaluated decision, not the changing rule implementation. Returning the rule revision makes the decision interpretable while keeping assignment consistent across app versions.
feedback.details:
Treat evaluation as a query over the authenticated account, feature key and server-owned rule revision. The response carries the evaluated result and revision; the client does not independently reproduce the rollout rule. Shipping percentages and bucketing code lets old clients continue using stale logic after operations changes the rule, while random local assignment is not account-stable. This contract does not promise that every device sees a new decision instantly; any decision-cache lifetime must be specified separately if required.

Boundary and reversal: If the rollout rule becomes a public, immutable client-side configuration and all active clients can update together, distributing it can be appropriate; neither condition holds in this scenario.

messages.text: Old clients can retain obsolete rules, so one account may receive inconsistent decisions during rollout.
The result is not tied to the account or the service’s current assignment rule.

replacements.learningObjective: Specify time-window boundaries and timezone offsets in the appointment search contract so adjacent slots are not duplicated or skipped.

question.prompt: A scheduling client partitions a date range into adjacent appointment searches. A slot starting exactly at a shared boundary belongs to the later search, and clients may query during a daylight-saving fall-back.
constraints: Clients can send timestamps with an explicit UTC offset.
Adjacent searches must cover every slot start once, with a boundary-start slot in the later range.
The repeated local hour during a daylight-saving fall-back names two possible instants.

options.text: Normalize explicit-offset timestamps to instants and include the start while excluding the end.
Accept local wall-clock times and use the server’s configured zone to choose an instant for each query.
Include both endpoints and return slots touching a range boundary, then deduplicate the results in the client.

feedback.reason: Explicit offsets identify instants even when local civil time repeats during daylight-saving fall-back. A half-open range includes its start and excludes its end, so a slot on a shared endpoint appears only once across adjacent queries.
feedback.details:
Normalize query bounds to instants using the explicit offset supplied by the caller. A half-open range includes its start and excludes its end, so a slot on a shared endpoint appears only in the next adjacent query. Offset-free local time can be ambiguous during the daylight-saving fall-back hour; rejecting it unless the caller supplies the intended offset avoids choosing an instant silently. If the business defines a different boundary convention, it must be used consistently by storage, search and clients.

Boundary and reversal: If the product wants end-inclusive ranges, callers must advance the next range past the prior endpoint and the contract must state that behavior; the adjacent-slot premise favors half-open ranges.

messages.text: The same request can identify different instants across servers or daylight-saving transitions.
A slot ending at 10:15 and the next beginning at 10:15 both match the shared boundary.

replacements.learningObjective: Bind search pagination to one query snapshot so records changing between page requests do not create duplicates or gaps.

question.prompt: A discovery API returns large search results in pages. New records and index updates can occur while a user follows the next-page link. The client expects a stable traversal for the same search request.
constraints: The index can change between page requests.
The API can retain a snapshot token for the cursor lifetime.
The query and sort order are part of the pagination identity.

options.text: Bind the opaque cursor to the query, sort order and retained index snapshot; require it on the next-page request.
Use a numeric offset against the live index and rebuild ordering for each page, accepting shifts as records arrive.
Return pages without a snapshot and ask each client to remove repeated IDs after it finishes traversing them.

feedback.reason: A snapshot-bound cursor holds the query and ordering stable across page requests. Offsets into a changing index can shift, and client deduplication cannot restore omitted records.
feedback.details:
The cursor is a continuation contract, not just an encoded row number. It should bind the normalized filter, sort keys and an index snapshot or equivalent stable boundary; it can expire with an explicit restart response. A live offset is simpler when the collection is static, but this index changes during traversal. Deduplicating IDs only removes repeated rows and cannot reveal an item skipped when earlier rows moved. If the product accepts a live, best-effort feed instead of a stable traversal, its cursor semantics should say so.

Boundary and reversal: If the index cannot retain snapshots, use a stable keyset cursor over a monotonic ordering field and document which concurrent inserts may be excluded.

messages.text: Insertions or removals before the offset can shift results and cause gaps or duplicates.
Deduplication can hide duplicates but cannot recover omitted results or establish a stable view.

replacements.learningObjective: Apply per-tenant concurrency admission to expensive route solves and return a retryable capacity outcome instead of silently queueing unbounded work.

question.prompt: A route-planning service has capacity for six solves. Two tenants may each use three at once, but no tenant may exceed three; excess requests are not queued.
constraints: The total service can run six solves concurrently.
Each tenant has a separate limit of three in-flight solves.
The client can retry after a capacity rejection.

options.text: Admit three concurrent solves per tenant; reject excess requests with a capacity status and retry delay, without queueing them.
Accept every request into a queue and retain excess solve inputs until workers catch up.
Limit only the whole service to six concurrent solves, with no per-tenant counter.

feedback.reason: A per-tenant in-flight limit enforces the stated admission rule. Excess work must be rejected rather than represented as accepted background work, and a retry hint tells callers when to try again.
feedback.details:
Admission needs both the aggregate six-solve ceiling and each tenant’s three-solve ceiling. A tenant-scoped counter enforces the latter while shared capacity enforces the former. Excess work is rejected rather than represented as queued; a retry hint can tell clients when to try again. A global-only cap of three would reject work even when the remaining capacity is available to another tenant. No additional fairness or priority policy is implied.

Boundary and reversal: If callers require eventual execution instead of retrying, change the contract to an explicitly bounded queue with an operation resource and queue-capacity outcome.

messages.text: This moves overload into retained work and violates the explicit no-unbounded-waiting constraint.
One tenant could take four slots, exceeding its stated limit while service capacity remains available.

replacements.learningObjective: Define machine-readable problem types for invalid payment input, a definitive issuer decline, and temporary capacity rejection without making clients parse human text.

question.prompt: A payment authorization API can reject a malformed amount, receive a definitive issuer decline, or refuse work because its own capacity limit is reached. Clients must correct, stop, or retry differently for those three outcomes.
constraints: The issuer decline is a final known result.
Capacity rejection means the authorization was not submitted to the issuer.
Human-readable text may be localized and can change.

options.text: Use HTTP status plus a stable Problem Details type for invalid input, decline and capacity; add retry guidance only for capacity.
Put the category in explanatory prose and ask clients to match words such as “declined” or “busy” in that text.
Return the same success status for all three outcomes and encode the result only in a human-readable response message.

feedback.reason: Stable problem types let callers distinguish correction, final decline, and retryable capacity rejection without parsing text. The HTTP status still communicates the general response class.
feedback.details:
RFC 9457 defines a problem-details format for machine-readable HTTP error details, including a problem type identifier and occurrence-specific explanation. Keep the issuer decline definitive, identify a malformed request as client-correctable, and make the service’s capacity rejection distinct from an issuer result. A Retry-After hint belongs only where the service actually expects a later retry. Detail text helps a person but should not be a protocol field clients parse. If an authorization can have an unknown external outcome, that requires a separate operation/reconciliation contract; this scenario deliberately excludes that condition.

Boundary and reversal: If the processor later adds a timeout with unknown charge outcome, do not map it into these three types; add an explicit unresolved outcome and reconciliation path.

messages.text: Localized or revised prose is not a stable machine contract.
Generic HTTP consumers cannot distinguish a failed authorization from a successful response.

replacements.learningObjective: Evolve the fraud-case response additively while old and new workers coexist, preserving existing enum meanings and required fields.

question.prompt: A fraud case API is rolling out a new optional `reviewReason` field. Old and new workers will run concurrently for several days, and existing consumers require the current status field and values.
constraints: Old workers ignore unknown response fields.
The existing `status` values retain their meanings.
The new field is informative and not required for existing case handling.

options.text: Add `reviewReason` as optional data and preserve the existing status field and enum values throughout the overlap.
Add the new reason by changing existing status values to encode both state and reason.
Deploy all consumers at once and make `reviewReason` required in the same release.

feedback.reason: An optional additive field allows the overlap period without changing the status contract old workers depend on. The new reason remains supplemental rather than a prerequisite for handling the case.
feedback.details:
Compatibility must hold in both directions for the deployed readers and writers. Old workers can ignore a new optional field; they cannot safely reinterpret an existing status value that has acquired a second meaning. Keeping the field optional also means an older producer can still send a valid case while deployment rolls forward. A coordinated breaking migration is possible only if the system can actually cut over together, which the scenario rules out. If the reason changes authorization or routing, it is no longer merely informative and needs its own compatibility treatment.

Boundary and reversal: If every consumer can be drained and upgraded before the new field becomes required, a versioned breaking change becomes feasible; the several-day coexistence premise rules that out.

messages.text: Existing consumers may misread a value whose meaning changed.
The stated mixed-version window makes simultaneous replacement unavailable.

replacements.learningObjective: Address an export by an immutable snapshot that pins the payroll period, source watermark, and rules revision used to produce it.

question.prompt: A finance operator reruns a payroll export after a network failure. Source records may be corrected later, and tax rules can be revised; an audit must reproduce the same export that was approved originally.
constraints: The export is an audit artifact once approved.
The source can change after export creation.
The applicable payroll-rules revision is identifiable.

options.text: Create an immutable export resource pinned to period, source watermark and rules revision; retrieval returns that artifact.
Make the same period URL recalculate from current rows and current rules on every GET.
Ask finance to save the first file locally and treat later server output as an unrelated export.

feedback.reason: The approved export must be an immutable resource tied to its input boundary and rules revision. A later retry retrieves the artifact instead of silently recalculating a different one.
feedback.details:
At creation, record the payroll period, the source watermark or equivalent snapshot boundary, and the rules revision. Give the result an export identity and make subsequent retrieval return the same bytes or a clearly versioned derivative. A latest-data query is useful for a new export but cannot reproduce an earlier approval. Local copies may be useful evidence, yet they do not replace the server’s association between approved inputs and generated output. If corrections require a new official export, issue a new export identity and supersede the prior one explicitly.

Boundary and reversal: If audit policy requires a corrected export to replace the approved one, represent that as a new revision with a link to the superseded artifact.

messages.text: A retry can return a different artifact for the same apparent export identity.
This provides no durable server-side identity or audit link to the approved result.

replacements.learningObjective: Keep a short-lived copy of low-sensitivity notification preferences in the signed-in client because local reuse is sufficient and cross-device sharing is not required.

question.prompt: A notification screen reads a user’s preferences repeatedly. They are low sensitivity, may be up to five minutes stale, and do not need to be shared between devices; writes still go to the preference service.
constraints: The user is signed in and the client knows the authenticated account.
Five minutes of staleness is acceptable for this screen.
The cache is for repeated reads on one device; writes remain server-owned.

options.text: Keep a private five-minute preference copy keyed to the signed-in account; send edits through the preference service.
Cache by URL at a shared edge and reuse the response for all callers for five minutes.
Treat the device copy as authoritative and accept preference changes locally without synchronizing the service.

feedback.reason: A private device cache meets the stated single-device reuse and five-minute freshness needs while keeping the service authoritative for writes. A shared URL key could mix users, and local-only writes would create a second authority.
feedback.details:
The cache belongs at the client because repeated reads are local and cross-device sharing is unnecessary. Scope it to the authenticated account and discard it at account change; the five-minute bound controls how long the screen may reuse it. Sending edits to the service preserves one write owner. A shared edge is not safe merely because the URL is stable, and a durable client-only record cannot satisfy the service’s role for other devices. If the UI later promises immediate cross-device preference visibility, this placement would need a shared validated read path or shorter freshness bound.

Boundary and reversal: If preferences become security-sensitive or must change across devices immediately, stop reusing this client copy until the stronger authorization and freshness requirements are satisfied.

messages.text: The key does not isolate user-specific preferences.
The cache becomes a second write authority, so other devices and server workflows can diverge.

replacements.learningObjective: Invalidate a read-heavy shipment projection from the committed update event instead of relying on periodic expiry.

question.prompt: A tracking service serves high-volume reads from a parcel cache because the origin permits one refresh per parcel per 20 seconds. The authoritative write publishes a parcel-specific invalidation before it acknowledges the update.
constraints: Each cache entry is keyed by parcel ID.
A committed tracking update produces a reliable invalidation for that parcel before the write response succeeds.
The origin read budget requires unchanged parcel entries to remain reusable between refreshes.

options.text: Evict by parcel on each committed update; keep a 20-second TTL as fallback.
Keep the old parcel value until its full 20-second lifetime expires, then fetch the current projection.
Clear every shipment entry on each parcel read so no cached projection can survive any lookup.

feedback.reason: Because the invalidation is committed before the update is acknowledged, targeted eviction makes the next read observe the new projection. The maximum age remains a recovery bound rather than the primary freshness mechanism.
feedback.details:
The event is tied to the authoritative commit and names the changed parcel, so the cache can evict exactly that entry. A fixed TTL alone permits an acknowledged update to remain hidden for the rest of the 20-second window. Flushing all parcels on every read creates broad cache churn and still does not provide a clearer update boundary than the guaranteed event. The TTL protects against an entry surviving because it was never touched by a later event; it is not the normal update path. If event delivery were merely best effort, this immediate-after-acknowledgement guarantee would not be valid.

Boundary and reversal: If the source cannot guarantee invalidation before acknowledging writes, use a bounded stale-read contract or an explicit version check; do not claim read-after-acknowledgement from best-effort events.

messages.text: A read immediately after a successful update would return the prior parcel state.
This throws away reuse for unrelated parcels and does not use the targeted committed event.

replacements.learningObjective: Reuse immutable extraction output by a key that includes the input digest and extractor version, while keeping tenant-private documents isolated.

question.prompt: A document processor receives identical files more than once. Extraction output is deterministic for a given file and extractor version, but files are tenant-private and a new extractor release can change results.
constraints: The file has a stable content digest.
The extractor version is recorded with every result.
Results must not be shared across tenant boundaries.

options.text: Cache the immutable result by tenant, content digest, and extractor version; reuse only when all three match.
Cache globally by filename and reuse the result regardless of tenant or extractor release.
Cache only by job ID, so every repeat upload creates a new key and repeats extraction.

feedback.reason: Tenant, content digest and extractor version together identify a reusable result. Omitting tenant risks cross-tenant disclosure; omitting the version can serve output produced by different logic.
feedback.details:
The processor can reuse an immutable derived artifact because the input and transformation are fixed. The tenant component prevents one tenant’s cache entry from satisfying another tenant’s request, the digest identifies the bytes, and the extractor version distinguishes changed transformations. A filename is not content identity, and a job ID identifies an attempt rather than reusable work. This design assumes the result itself remains within the tenant boundary; if extracted data has additional user-level permissions, include that scope or reauthorize before returning it.

Boundary and reversal: If extraction becomes nondeterministic or depends on an external reference not captured in the key, either add that input to the key or stop reusing the result.

messages.text: Names can collide, tenant data can leak, and the result may come from old processing logic.
This key cannot identify deterministic work shared by repeated inputs.

replacements.learningObjective: Cache immutable venue layout separately from exact seat availability so static traffic does not freeze a changing inventory fact.

question.prompt: A ticket page serves a venue seat map and current seat availability. Layout changes only by published layout version; availability changes after every sale and must be exact when displayed. The origin limits layout downloads, but availability can be fetched from its owning service.
constraints: A layout is immutable within a published venue-layout version.
The origin cannot serve the repeated static layout traffic directly.
Availability changes independently and must be fetched from its authority for each display.

options.text: Cache layout by venue/version; read availability live on each display.
Cache layout and availability together under venue ID until the next layout release.
Fetch both layout and availability from origin for every display.

feedback.reason: Versioning gives the static layout a stable shared identity, while current availability has a separate owner and must not inherit that cache lifetime.
feedback.details:
Cache only the immutable layout artifact, using venue and published layout version as its identity. Read current availability from the availability owner for each display because sales can change it without a layout release. Combining those values makes the exact, mutable part stale; bypassing layout reuse sends traffic to an origin that cannot serve it. This is a cache-placement and data-separation decision, not a claim that the cached layout reserves seats. If the product later accepts bounded-stale availability, it can define a separate estimate cache without changing the layout contract.

Boundary and reversal: If the availability service later allows a documented freshness window, a separate availability projection may be cached within that bound; it must remain independent from the immutable seat-map artifact.

messages.text: Sales change availability without changing the layout version.
The origin cannot serve the repeated layout traffic, and the layout is safely reusable by version.

replacements.learningObjective: Cache only tenant-scoped candidate case IDs and recheck each case’s current per-agent authorization before returning case content.

question.prompt: Support search spans cases within a tenant. Agents have different case permissions, and permission changes must take effect on the next response; the search index can return candidate IDs separately from case content.
constraints: Candidate IDs can be shared within one tenant.
Case-level authorization differs by agent and can change immediately.
The case service can authorize each candidate before returning its contents.

options.text: Cache tenant/query candidate IDs; fetch each case and authorize it for the current agent.
Cache the final case documents by tenant and query and reuse them for any agent in that tenant.
Cache final results by agent ID with no permission-version check or expiry.

feedback.reason: The search candidate set is reusable within a tenant, but disclosure is agent-specific and must be checked on each response. Caching IDs and reauthorizing content separates those two boundaries.
feedback.details:
Cache only the candidate identifiers under tenant and normalized query. Before returning any document, the case service checks the current agent’s rights; a cached ID cannot itself grant access. Caching the final document by tenant incorrectly assumes all agents share permissions. Keying by agent without a permission-version check or bounded invalidation still serves content after rights change. If the index itself contains sensitive snippets, even candidate caching needs narrower access controls; the scenario explicitly makes IDs shareable within the tenant.

Boundary and reversal: If the search index cannot safely expose candidate IDs across agents, scope candidate caching to the agent or move filtering into the authorized search boundary.

messages.text: Tenant membership alone does not grant every agent the same case access.
A permission change leaves the old result eligible for that agent.

replacements.learningObjective: Use conditional revalidation for frequently updated public metadata so edge copies can be reused briefly without presenting a representation beyond its freshness bound.

question.prompt: A media catalog serves a mutable public metadata URL worldwide. Titles can change several times a day, edge copies may be no more than 15 seconds stale, and the origin supplies a validator. The origin permits at most one full representation transfer per URL in each 15-second window; conditional validation is allowed.
constraints: The metadata is public and identical for all viewers.
The maximum stale age is 15 seconds.
The origin limits full transfers to one per URL per 15 seconds and supports conditional validation.

options.text: Cache for 15 seconds, then conditionally revalidate the origin before reuse.
Cache the mutable URL for a day and assume a purge will always reach each edge within 15 seconds.
Fetch a complete representation from origin on every request and ignore the supplied validator.

feedback.reason: A short freshness lifetime controls how long an edge may reuse the mutable copy without checking. After that, conditional revalidation can establish whether the stored representation remains current.
feedback.details:
The 15-second value belongs to the cache’s freshness policy for this mutable URL. Once it expires, the validator lets the edge ask whether the stored representation is still current and avoid retransferring unchanged bytes. The validator does not make an expired copy fresh by itself; the origin’s validation response does that. A long TTL plus hoped-for purges cannot guarantee the stated bound, and unconditional full fetches waste an available validation path. If the origin cannot be reached after expiry, the edge must follow an explicitly allowed stale-if-error policy; none is given here.

Boundary and reversal: If the product explicitly allows stale serving during origin failure, add a maximum stale-on-error window and expose that behavior; do not infer it from the normal 15-second bound.

messages.text: The given bound would depend on a best-effort invalidation reaching every location.
This discards conditional validation even though the origin can confirm an unchanged representation.

replacements.learningObjective: Cache immutable device capability manifests by model and firmware build, while fetching each device’s current operational state from its owning service.

question.prompt: A device portal displays supported features and protocol limits. Those capabilities are identical for devices on the same firmware build and do not change after release; connectivity and reported state are device-specific and can change at any moment.
constraints: A manifest is immutable for a model and firmware build.
Operational state is per-device and can change without a firmware change.
The portal can request manifest and operational state separately.

options.text: Cache manifests by model/build; fetch live device state separately.
Cache one manifest per model and keep using it after devices move to a different firmware build.
Cache manifest and connectivity together by model for the manifest lifetime.

feedback.reason: The manifest is shared and immutable only within a model/build pair. Device connectivity has a different owner and freshness requirement, so it must not inherit the manifest cache lifetime.
feedback.details:
A firmware build identifies the supported capabilities; the model alone may cover multiple builds. Cache that manifest broadly under both dimensions. Keep live connectivity and reported state on the device service path because two devices on the same build can differ, and a state change does not create a new manifest. Combining them lets a long-lived capability cache freeze operational facts. If a firmware build can change capabilities after publication, the manifest is not immutable and needs its own revision or revalidation rule.

Boundary and reversal: If the portal only needs a historic “last known state,” it can cache that separately with a timestamp and explicit age label; the current view described here must use live state.

messages.text: Capabilities can differ between firmware builds of the same model.
One device’s changing connectivity state is neither shared by model nor immutable.

replacements.learningObjective: Keep unsent document edits in a client-local draft cache, but identify the server revision they were based on before attempting to publish them.

question.prompt: A document editor must survive browser refresh while offline. The server remains authoritative, and another collaborator may edit the same document before this client reconnects.
constraints: The local draft must survive a refresh on the same device.
The client can retain the server revision read before going offline.
Conflicting edits must not silently overwrite the server version.

options.text: Keep the draft and base revision locally; submit conditionally after reconnect and show a conflict if changed.
Treat the local draft cache as the latest shared document and overwrite the server after reconnect.
Never retain a local copy and require the user to keep the page open until connectivity returns.

feedback.reason: The client cache protects unsent work, while the saved base revision allows the server to detect a conflict before publication. Local persistence is not evidence that the shared document is current.
feedback.details:
Keep the draft and its base revision together. After reconnection, submit with that version as a precondition; if the server has advanced, preserve the local draft and ask the user to merge rather than overwriting. The local cache is appropriate because the requirement is same-device recovery. It must not become a second shared authority, and discarding it loses work. If the editor supports automatic merges, apply its documented merge algorithm only after detecting the concurrent version.

Boundary and reversal: If the product explicitly chooses last-write-wins for this document type, it can omit conflict UI, but that would replace the stated no-silent-overwrite requirement.

messages.text: Offline state may be older than another collaborator’s saved revision.
The explicit refresh/offline requirement is not met.

replacements.learningObjective: Cache the immutable road graph by graph release and region, but read live closures separately so a cached map cannot conceal a current restriction.

question.prompt: A route planner reads road topology and traffic restrictions from separate sources. Topology changes only in versioned releases, while closures may change every minute and must be reflected in previews within 30 seconds.
constraints: The road graph is immutable within a published release.
Live closure data has a 30-second maximum age.
The route response can identify the graph release and closure observation time.

options.text: Cache graph by region/release; refresh closure data within 30 seconds and return both timestamps.
Cache a complete route with graph and closure assumptions for a day using only the origin and destination as key.
Fetch the same immutable graph release from origin on every preview and ignore the separate closure timestamp.

feedback.reason: The graph release is safe to reuse by region and version; live closures are not. Keeping their cache lifetimes and timestamps separate prevents a current restriction from being hidden by a static topology cache.
feedback.details:
Build the route from separately identified inputs. Region plus graph release selects an immutable topology artifact, while closure observations refresh under the 30-second bound and carry their own timestamp. A single route cache keyed only by endpoints omits both dimensions and can conceal new restrictions. Fetching graph tiles on every call is unnecessary, and doing so does not solve stale closure data unless that source is separately checked. If a route response cannot show which topology and closure observation it used, downstream users cannot tell whether a route is still valid.

Boundary and reversal: If live restrictions must take effect faster than 30 seconds, tighten that source’s bound or add an authoritative route-validation step; do not shorten the immutable graph cache for that purpose.

messages.text: A changed graph release or a new closure can make the cached route unsafe.
This wastes safe static reuse while still failing to enforce the changing input’s freshness bound.

replacements.learningObjective: Reuse a materialized forecast only when its facility set, horizon and calculation revision match the request, and return the data watermark so planners know what it includes.

question.prompt: A warehouse planner runs expensive forecasts over selected facilities and time horizons. Many planners request the same report; stock changes are incorporated every ten minutes, and forecast rules can be revised independently of stock data.
constraints: Forecast output depends on selected facility set and time horizon.
Stock movement data is refreshed every ten minutes.
Forecast rules have an explicit revision.

options.text: Key by facility set, horizon, and rule revision; refresh per stock batch and return its watermark.
Reuse the latest forecast under one shared report name regardless of facilities, horizon or rule revision.
Recompute from every facility’s live movements for each planner request and omit the rules revision from the result.

feedback.reason: The forecast is a reusable derived report only when its dimensions and rules match. Its watermark communicates stock-data progress independently of the cache age.
feedback.details:
Normalize the facility set and horizon into the cache key and include the rule revision because it changes the computation. Refresh the materialized result as new stock movement batches are incorporated; its watermark says which batch is represented. A generic report-name key silently mixes different planner questions, while live recomputation repeats the expensive aggregation and still cannot explain which rules version produced it. This item concerns the identity and provenance of a read model, not whether the forecast can authorize a stock pick.

Boundary and reversal: If planners require a forecast based on a specific later watermark, wait for that source watermark or return that it is not yet available instead of relabeling an older result.

messages.text: Different planner requests and rule versions can receive the wrong aggregate.
This repeats expensive work and still leaves the report’s calculation version unclear.

replacements.learningObjective: Cache a public course catalog by release version while retrieving learner-specific progress through its authorized service path.

question.prompt: A learning app serves the same course outline to every learner, but completion progress is private and changes after each saved lesson. Course releases have immutable version IDs, and the human-readable course URL can move to a newer release.
constraints: Course outline content is public and immutable within a release.
Progress belongs to one learner and changes on completion.
The course URL may point to a different release later; progress can be requested separately.

options.text: Cache the course outline by immutable release ID; fetch progress from the learner service under the current identity.
Cache the combined outline-and-progress response by course ID and reuse it for all learners.
Cache the outline by human-readable course URL across a release change, and keep the old outline under that alias.

feedback.reason: The two payloads have different owners and sharing rules. The immutable outline can be shared by release ID; learner progress must be fetched through its authorized path.
feedback.details:
Split the response at the data boundary. A public outline is immutable for a release, so its release ID is a safe shared cache key. Progress is learner-specific and mutable, so it must be retrieved under the current identity and must not ride in a course-wide cache entry. Caching the combined payload by course ID would leak or misstate progress. Avoiding all caching is unnecessary for the public part. If the course outline itself becomes personalized, it must leave the shared cache or include the personalization scope in its key.

Boundary and reversal: If progress has a documented local freshness allowance, the app may add a private learner-scoped cache with that explicit bound; none is specified here.

messages.text: The cache mixes one learner’s private state with another learner’s response.
The alias can move while release IDs remain immutable, so it does not identify one outline version.

replacements.learningObjective: Publish public prices under immutable revision URLs and keep checkout on the authoritative current-price path for final acceptance.

question.prompt: A merchant publishes product prices to a global catalog. Browsing may show a price pointer that is 15 seconds old, but checkout must reject a quote if the effective price changed before acceptance.
constraints: Published price revisions are immutable and public.
The browsing pointer may lag 15 seconds.
Checkout can revalidate the revision before accepting payment.

options.text: Cache immutable prices by revision; bound the pointer to 15 seconds and revalidate at checkout.
Cache one mutable product URL for hours and let checkout accept whichever price the edge returns.
Assume every edge purge completes before publication succeeds and skip checkout revalidation.

feedback.reason: Immutable revision URLs support safe edge reuse, while the mutable listing pointer has the stated 15-second bound. Checkout must still verify the effective revision before accepting payment.
feedback.details:
Browsing and buying have different guarantees. The edge can cache a revision that never changes and resolve the current pointer within its 15-second limit. The checkout service then checks that the quote’s revision is still effective before accepting payment, so a stale browse response cannot silently charge the wrong current price. Depending on purge propagation as the only correctness mechanism overstates what the system knows. If the business honors any shown price even after publication changes, checkout’s revalidation policy must reflect that contractual promise instead.

Boundary and reversal: If the merchant contract guarantees the displayed price for a quote lifetime, checkout should validate that quote’s pinned revision rather than require the latest catalog revision.

messages.text: A stale edge copy can set the accepted payment amount beyond the allowed 15-second browse lag.
The scenario states only a bounded pointer lag, not a globally synchronous purge guarantee.

replacements.learningObjective: Bound any authorization cache from a non-lagging identity source by the five-second revocation objective, and fail closed when current state cannot be established.

question.prompt: An identity directory checks whether a credential is active. Its authoritative store reflects revocations immediately; authorization reads do not use a lagging replica. A protected request must be rejected within five seconds after the revocation is committed.
constraints: The authoritative identity store reflects a revocation immediately; authorization reads do not use a lagging replica.
A protected request must be rejected within five seconds after revocation commit.
If current credential state is unavailable, the protected request must not be authorized.

options.text: Cache status for at most five seconds; deny when freshness is unknown.
Cache active status for an hour and continue accepting requests while the identity service is down.
On status lookup failure treat the credential as active to preserve availability.

feedback.reason: The cache lifetime cannot exceed the five-second revocation objective, and a lookup failure must not grant access. A longer positive cache would violate the stated limit.
feedback.details:
If the system caches credential status, the maximum age and invalidation path must fit within the five-second bound. On expiry or source failure, the service cannot know that the credential is still active, so it rejects or defers the protected operation according to its error contract. A long positive cache leaves revoked credentials usable; fail-open behavior makes a dependency outage an authorization decision. This may reduce availability, which is the explicit consequence of the requirement. If the product chooses a longer revocation window, state that policy change rather than silently extending cache TTL.

Boundary and reversal: If the operation is non-sensitive and the product explicitly allows bounded stale authorization, define that separate exception and do not apply it to the protected operation in this scenario.

messages.text: A credential revoked during that hour remains usable beyond the stated bound.
This turns unknown state into permission despite the fail-closed requirement.

replacements.learningObjective: Cache transcoded artifacts by immutable input digest and complete encoding recipe so a changed source or codec setting cannot reuse the wrong output.

question.prompt: A media workflow stores public renditions produced from source files. Outputs are deterministic for a fixed source digest, codec version, resolution and encoding settings; source replacements must become visible as new outputs.
constraints: Each source file has a content digest.
The full encoding recipe and codec version are recorded.
Published outputs are immutable and public.

options.text: Key by source digest and full encoding recipe; publish the output immutably.
Cache by asset name alone and overwrite the cached output when a worker finishes.
Cache the job submission response and return it as if it were the completed rendition.

feedback.reason: The output identity must include the source content and the full transformation recipe. An immutable result can then be shared safely; asset name or job ID alone cannot identify its bytes.
feedback.details:
Include the source digest, codec implementation version, resolution and every output-affecting setting in the key. A changed input or recipe creates a new immutable artifact instead of mutating a shared URL. Because these renditions are public, a CDN can reuse the artifact; the workflow’s job status remains a separate resource from the output. Caching by asset name risks collisions across source replacements, and returning a cached submission response does not supply completed content. If outputs contain private overlays, the public-cache assumption no longer holds.

Boundary and reversal: If the encoder is nondeterministic or depends on uncaptured data, include the missing input or stop treating the result as content-addressable.

messages.text: A replacement source or changed recipe can collide with the old artifact.
An accepted job record is not the immutable output bytes.

replacements.learningObjective: Use a bounded edge cache for rollout configuration and make the emergency disable path meet the same 15-second staleness limit under failed invalidation.

question.prompt: Edge workers read a public, non-secret feature configuration. A value may be reused for at most 15 seconds; after expiry an unavailable origin means the feature must be treated as disabled. The origin allows at most one revalidation request per key during each 15-second window.
constraints: The configuration is identical across callers and is safe to share.
After its 15-second freshness window, an old enabled value must not be used if revalidation fails.
The origin caps revalidation to one request per key per 15-second window.

options.text: Cache 15 seconds, revalidate once after expiry, and disable on failure.
Bypass the cache and query the origin for every edge request, even when the current value is still fresh.
Continue serving an expired enabled value during a prolonged origin outage and revalidate in the background.

feedback.reason: A shared value can be reused for 15 seconds, but expiry requires one bounded revalidation and failure disables the feature. Neither repeated origin reads nor stale enabled reuse meets the stated constraints.
feedback.details:
Because the configuration is public and identical across callers, the edge can hold one shared value per key during its freshness window. After 15 seconds, a revalidation is needed; if the origin is unavailable, the worker treats the feature as disabled rather than using the old enabled value. Request coalescing at the key boundary respects the origin’s one-request budget. This is a cache-freshness and failure decision, not an assertion that push invalidation is reliable. If configuration were secret or tenant-specific, the sharing scope would change.

Boundary and reversal: If a faster emergency-disable objective is needed, state it separately and support it with a verified invalidation path; the 15-second freshness window does not imply a stronger guarantee.

messages.text: This exceeds the origin limit of one revalidation per key in each 15-second window.
An expired value is explicitly unusable when revalidation fails.

replacements.learningObjective: Cache read-only appointment availability by provider and time window, but invalidate on schedule changes and recheck the authoritative slot when confirming a booking.

question.prompt: A calendar screen shows open appointment slots for a provider. The display may be 30 seconds old, booking changes emit an invalidation event, and a confirmed booking must never overlap another confirmed booking for that provider.
constraints: The calendar is a read-only availability projection.
Schedule changes normally invalidate affected provider/time-window entries.
The booking service can recheck and claim a slot atomically.

options.text: Cache by provider/window for 30 seconds; evict on change and claim atomically at booking.
Treat an open slot in the cache as a reservation and confirm it without checking the booking record.
Cache one availability response for all providers and time windows because the display may be stale.

feedback.reason: A bounded projection is useful for browsing, but only the booking authority can claim a slot. Provider/window keys permit targeted invalidation, and the atomic recheck protects the no-overlap invariant.
feedback.details:
Build the read cache around the schedule dimensions that determine its contents: provider and time window. An update can evict affected entries early, while the 30-second maximum age remains the fallback if invalidation is delayed. On confirmation, the booking service checks current schedule state and creates the booking atomically. A cached open slot is not a hold. A global cache key erases the provider and time context, and a cache-as-lock can admit conflicting requests. If the product wants to hold a slot during checkout, create a separate expiring hold with an authoritative identity.

Boundary and reversal: If the business promises that a displayed slot is reserved for a user, add a durable expiring-hold contract instead of treating the availability cache as a reservation.

messages.text: Two users can act on the same stale open-slot result.
The key merges distinct schedules and cannot identify which change should invalidate it.

replacements.learningObjective: Coalesce concurrent refreshes for the same expensive public query while serving a bounded stale result during one refresh.

question.prompt: A public trending-search query is expensive to compute. Identical requests for the same normalized query and locale often arrive together; the service permits one refresh per key at a time and allows a result to be up to 20 seconds old.
constraints: The response is public and identical for the same normalized query and locale.
At most one origin refresh may run for a cache key at a time.
A previously computed result may be served until it is 20 seconds old while one refresh is in progress.

options.text: Key by normalized query/locale; coalesce one refresh and serve the prior result for at most 20 seconds.
Start a separate origin computation for every simultaneous request, even when query and locale match.
Use one shared result for every query and locale until any request triggers a refresh.

feedback.reason: Per-key coalescing respects the origin’s single-refresh limit while the 20-second age bound permits concurrent readers to receive the last result during refresh.
feedback.details:
Normalize query and locale before constructing the key, then maintain one in-flight refresh for that key. Concurrent callers can await its result or receive the prior response if it remains inside the stated 20-second window. The key must not collapse distinct searches, and starting one computation per caller would exceed the origin limit during a traffic spike. This item concerns duplicate-work control for a read-only result; it does not claim a snapshot across multiple search pages or a source watermark. If the prior result is older than 20 seconds and refresh fails, return the defined unavailable outcome rather than extending its age silently.

Boundary and reversal: If each request carries caller-specific filters or authorization, include those dimensions in the key or avoid sharing the response; the scenario only permits sharing a public normalized query.

messages.text: This violates the one-refresh-per-key limit and multiplies the expensive work.
Different normalized queries can have different results and cannot share one cache key.
